# Beyond Parental Wealth: Grandparental Wealth and the Transition to Adulthood

**Authors:** Emma Zang; Christina Gibson-Davis; Haolun Li

**Affiliations:** Department of Sociology, Yale University | Sanford School of Public Policy, Duke University | Department of Economics, Princeton University

## Abstract

This study considers the multigenerational consequences of wealth transmission for the transition to young adulthood. Using a wider set of outcomes than has previously been considered, and by analyzing parental and grandparental wealth simultaneously, this work underscores the salience of multiple generations of wealth as a predictor for young adult well-being. Data comes from the US Panel Study of Income Dynamics on a sample of youth followed from mid-adolescence until the age of 20. Results from linear regression models indicate that parental wealth was associated with increases in the probability of college attendance and steady employment and inversely associated with the likelihood of nonmarital birth and idleness. Grandparental wealth predicted non-educational outcomes at least as well as parental wealth did and explained more variance in young adults’ outcomes when parental wealth was lower. The association between parental wealth and non-educational outcomes suggest that wealth may inform young adults’ broader life course by predicting outcomes other than college attendance. Grandparental wealth may serve a compensatory function for children with low parental wealth. Results suggest that persistently low wealth across multiple generations may impede the successful transition to young adulthood.

## Introduction

Economic support from family and kin is a crucial resource for adolescents transitioning to adulthood (Fingerman et al. 2015; Kirkpatrick Johnson 2013). Young adults may use these resources to ease the risks and uncertainty accompanying early adulthood, when education, employment, and relationships are in flux (Furstenberg Jr 2010; Hartnett et al. 2013). Familial resource provision is positively correlated with young adults’ human capital attainment, employment success, and financial independence (Johnson and Benson 2012; Rauscher 2016).

Research has typically measured these economic supports in terms of parental income (Fingerman et al. 2015; Kirkpatrick Johnson 2013), but wealth (or net worth) may be an equally important source of support (Addo et al. 2016; Killewald et al. 2017; Shanks and Destin 2009). As a cumulative stock of resources, wealth likely has instrumental, psychological, and symbolic functions for young adults that speak to parents’ investment abilities, ease psychological strain, inform social class membership, and scaffold future expectations and opportunities (Diemer et al. 2020; Elliott et al. 2011; Gibson-Davis and Hill 2021; Sherraden 1991). The literature on parental wealth and young adults has focused primarily on educational outcomes, finding that net of parental income, parental wealth is positively correlated with college attendance and graduation (Conley 2001; Jez 2014; Pfeffer 2018). However, the predictive value of parental wealth is unlikely to be confined to young adults’ educational attainment. Insofar as wealth speaks to class membership and endows cultural and social capital, parental wealth is likely to inform other aspects of the life course trajectory of young adults, including decisions related to employment and fertility.

An investigation of how parental wealth informs young adult children’s life chances, though, is likely to understate wealth’s role unless grandparental wealth is considered. Theoretical models highlight grandchildren’s embeddedness in a larger network of kin (Allen et al. 2019) and suggest that child-centric resources are inadequately measured if only the parent–child dyad is considered (Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017; Mare 2011). Given that grandparental and parental wealth are relatively modestly correlated (0.41; Pfeffer and Killewald 2018) and that in vivo transmission of wealth from grandparent to grandchild is common (Killewald and Bryan 2018), grandparental wealth may be an important but overlooked source of support in emerging adulthood.

Wealth in the United States is highly racialized, with Black families having less than $0.01 in wealth for every $1.00 of wealth held by White families (Gibson-Davis and Hill 2021). These vast disparities in wealth reflect long-standing and entrenched patterns of structural inequality and institutional racism that have impeded wealth acquisition for Black Americans (Darity Jr and Mullen 2020; Oliver and Shapiro 1995). Given the cumulative nature of wealth and its transmission from one generation to the next, Black, relative to White, young adults, have less wealthy parents and grandparents (Nam 2020; Pfeffer and Killewald 2019). White parents and grandparents also have different asset and debt portfolios than do Black parents and grandparents (Addo and Lichter 2013; Bandelj and Grigoryeva 2021), potentially influencing the types of resources that they can offer their children and grandchildren. At the same time, the association between wealth and Black child and youth well-being is complicated, with studies indicating a less robust association between wealth and outcomes than might otherwise be expected (Conwell and Ye 2021; Kaushal and Nepomnyaschy 2009; Yeung and Conley 2008). Because of this complexity, and for the sake of focus, our study does not focus on Black-White differences in wealth, with the exception of some supplementary analyses discussed at the end. We acknowledge that the importance of the American racialization of wealth, but felt that a complete examination of this multifaceted topic beyond the scope of this study.

In this study, we investigate whether differences in parental and grandparental wealth predict the quality of the transition to adulthood as measured by four indicators: college attendance, lack of idleness, steady employment, and the absence of an early nonmarital birth. We use data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) for 1968–2019 and conduct linear regressions to model the relationship between family wealth and outcomes. We observe parental wealth when individuals were aged 12–16 and observe young adult outcomes at age 20.

Our work makes several important contributions. First, we build on and extend previous studies demonstrating that wealth is positively associated with human capital attainment for young adults (Conley 2001; Jez 2014; Pfeffer 2018) by considering a broader set of outcomes in young adulthood. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to consider parental wealth’s association with employment, idleness, and nonmarital fertility for young adults (for an examination of non-marital fertility over age 30, see Brady et al. 2020). Wealth does more than facilitate parental investment in educational goods. Wealth serves instrumental functions that determine access to resources and opportunities; it also serves symbolic and psychological functions that shape patterns of thinking and behaviors. The instrumental, psychological, and symbolic functions of wealth suggest it may play a broader role in the transition to adulthood than previously considered.

Second, by providing the first estimates of how parental and grandparental wealth are independently and jointly associated with young adult well-being, we speak to the potential multigenerational repercussions of wealth inequality. Research has shown that net of parental wealth, grandparental wealth can independently predict grandchildren’s wealth (Adermon et al. 2018; Pfeffer and Killewald 2018) and income levels (Toney and Robertson 2021). Evidence from Sweden demonstrates associations between grandparent wealth and educational performance (Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017). Our study extends this line of research by examining other relevant outcomes for grandchildren when they transition into their adulthood. Moreover, our findings can shed light on the relative importance of parental versus grandparental wealth, as well as on how parental and grandparental wealth interact to shape the outcomes.

Finally, this study is one of few to examine the relationship between grandparental wealth and grandchild outcomes in the US (for a European study, see Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017). Most studies of grandparent resources rely on data from Nordic countries (e.g., Engzell et al. 2020). Relative to Nordic countries, however, the United States has a weaker social safety net. Therefore, grandparental and family wealth may be a more important resource in the American context.

## Background

### The Role of Parental Wealth in Early Adulthood

The transition to adulthood is a critical stage for acquiring human capital and setting one’s economic trajectory (Hogan and Astone 1986; Swartz 2009). Generally conceptualized as the ages between 18 and 25, this “emerging adulthood” stage (Arnett 2000; Arnett 2007) sees many individuals completing their formal education, obtaining their first full-time job, and establishing economic independence from their parents. Educational attainment and early employment experiences during young adulthood impact earnings, economic well-being, and fertility choices throughout adulthood (Ben-Porath 1967; Brand and Davis 2011). Thus, disparities in young adult experiences may contribute to lasting inequality across the life course (DiPrete and Eirich 2006; Elder 1998; Seltzer and Bianchi 2013).

Parental resources can play an important role in the transition to adulthood. Referred to as a “hidden” source of inequality (Swartz et al. 2011), parental resources are the psychological, logistical, and monetary support that parents give to their young adult offspring (Fingerman et al. 2009; Swartz 2009). During a phase of life when education, employment, and relationships are in flux, young adults may use these resources to ease the riskiness and uncertainty that accompany early adulthood (Furstenberg Jr 2010; Schoeni and Ross 2005). Parental resource provision has been positively correlated with their adult offspring’s human capital attainment, employment success, and wealth and income (Johnson and Benson 2012; Rauscher 2016).

Conventionally, research has used income to measure parental resources (Belley and Lochner 2007; Duncan et al. 2017; Ziol-Guest and Lee 2016). However, a large and growing literature suggests that parental wealth—a household’s assets minus its debts—also contributes to offspring well-being (Conwell and Ye 2021; Diemer et al. 2020; Miller et al. 2021). Income and wealth are partly distinguished by providing different types of economic resources: income is a flow of cash into the household (e.g., labor market earnings, public assistance income), whereas wealth represents a stock of resources (i.e., assets minus debts). These flows and stocks can theoretically complement one another. For example, income and wealth can predict levels of parental investment and parental stress. However, as explained in further detail later, wealth has functions beyond those of income. For example, wealth facilitates access to the credit market, represents goods (i.e., housing or savings) that young adults can draw on in a time of crisis, and shapes social class status throughout the young adult’s life course.

Parental wealth is likely an important predictor of outcomes in emerging adulthood, providing instrumental, psychological, and symbolic benefits (Gibson-Davis and Hill 2021). Instrumental benefits begin to accrue in childhood and include facilitating living in safe neighborhoods with access to high-quality schools and enabling in vivo transfers to provide educational goods and culturally enriching experiences (Killewald et al. 2017; Yellen 2016). Stores of wealth also allow parents to invest in their children should financial crises interrupt income flows (Yellen 2016). As they age, young adult children may utilize parental assets as collateral to secure loans and access credit markets, rely on parents to provide housing or material support, or call on parental savings to smooth consumption or income shortfalls (Rauscher 2016; Seltzer and Bianchi 2013).

Psychologically, parental wealth offers a hedge against the risks associated with the transition to adulthood (Shapiro 2004). Parental wealth can help adult offspring endure unemployment spells, income volatility, or relationship transitions (Settersten Jr and Ray 2010). Young adults who can rely on their parents’ wealth as a backstop may feel they have more freedom to attend college or pursue a risky career. Conversely, children of parents with low wealth levels may feel economic despair and hopelessness, thereby lowering the perceived opportunity costs of a nonmarital birth (Kearney and Levine 2014). Moreover, adolescents who do not think they can attend college or achieve a desirable career may pursue life meaning in other ways, such as by having a child out of wedlock (Edin and Kefalas 2005).

Wealth is also predictive of adult stress, anxiety, and physical health, and parents who have higher levels of psychosocial functioning may be better able to meet the needs of their young adult offspring (Deaton 2002; Killewald et al. 2017). Wealth may also lessen parental stress for those parents in the “sandwich generation”, who may be providing economic and psychological supports for both their offspring and parents (Fingerman et al. 2011; Steiner and Fletcher 2017). The stress of this dual caregiving role may be particularly acute in the United States, where supports for the elderly are comparatively weak.

Symbolically, wealth both determines and expresses class status (Conley 1999), which influences the subjective experiences of social and economic position, opportunity, and belonging. Symbols of class status shape how individuals—including children—are treated by others and perceive themselves in ways that influence behavior, academic achievement, and health (Destin et al. 2012; Goodman et al. 2000; Mistry et al. 2015). Wealthy families also tend to form social ties with other high-status individuals, creating an elite network of social contacts who can offer career mentorship, a head start on education, and other valuable resources. These social ties may also speak to what is normative for members of a given social class – young adults growing up in wealthier families may have less exposure to out-of-wedlock births or know of people who are neither in school nor employed.

An additional symbolic function is that wealth speaks to the “construction of future possibilities” (Sherraden 1991, pg 152), parents’ and children’s internalized expectations for possible life outcomes. For example, parental wealth may be correlated with normative expectations regarding college attendance, employment, and early adult fertility. Children in wealthier families may order their lives based on these normative expectations. For example, they may feel that college attendance and graduation is feasible, because they received either implicit or explicit messages from their parents that they are expected to attend college. In addition, they may take steps to avoid a non-marital birth, as a non-marital birth would complicate their ability to attend and complete college. Parental expectations can mediate the relationship between wealth and college outcomes (Elliott et al. 2011; Shanks and Destin 2009) and may be a stronger explanatory factor for the effects of wealth on educational attainment than parental income (Diemer et al. 2020).

The empirical literature on the role of wealth in the transition to young adulthood has largely concentrated on educational outcomes (Addo et al. 2016; Nam 2020; Rauscher 2016). Parental wealth is positively associated with high school graduation, college attendance, and college graduation (Conley 2001; Hardy and Marcotte 2020; Jez 2014). The magnitude of these effects can be large. For children’s college graduation rates, Pfeffer (2018) found a 49 percentage point difference between the bottom and top quintiles of parental wealth (11% vs. 60%). Consistent with the theoretical separation between income and wealth, these documented associations between wealth and human capital attainment were robust to the statistical inclusion of income (Jez 2014; Nam 2020; Pfeffer 2018).

Research on how parental wealth predicts other markers of young adulthood, such as employment or family formation choices, is thin. Concentrating on an older age range (30–43) than is the focus here, Brady et al. (2020) found that parental wealth was inversely correlated with single parenthood and positively correlated with the likelihood of being partnered. (They did not consider employment or idleness.) Their study is consistent with a larger literature finding that adults’ net worth predicts their fertility and marriage choices (Addo 2014; Eads and Tach 2016; Schneider 2011). Beyond the Brady et al. study, however, we are unaware of research examining the association between parental wealth and young adults’ employment and fertility choices.

We argue that a comprehensive understanding of the association between parental wealth and the transition to adulthood should consider a broader set of markers than previously considered. We think it likely that parental wealth influences outcomes beyond those that can be directly purchased (such as college education), and instead, through its psychological and symbolic functions, informs decisions regarding fertility and employment. Given that young adults are making important decisions not only in regard to human capital, but also in regards to employment and fertility, our study considers four outcomes that spans these areas. Although many of these markers, such as educational attainment and family formation choices, may be correlated, each captures a unique aspect of young adults’ life course.

### The Role of Grandparental Wealth

An additional but understudied predictor of young adult well-being is grandparental wealth. Not only is grandparental wealth an important determinant of parental wealth (Pfeffer and Killewald 2018), but it also represents a separate stream of potential resources for young adults. Indeed, grandparents likely have more wealth to offer their grandchildren than parents do: U.S. wealth levels peak for individuals of prime grandparent ages (65–74; Bhutta et al. 2019). The correlation between grandparental and parental wealth (measured at parental ages 45–64, when many parents likely have young adult children) is .41 (Pfeffer and Killewald 2018)—a modest association that suggest that parental wealth is not a simple statistical proxy for grandparental wealth. Moreover, as life spans have increased, many grandparents are alive when their grandchildren reach young adulthood. Longer life spans signify that grandparental wealth is independent of parental wealth insofar as grandparental wealth is rarely realized through inheritances. In our PSID sample, only around 7% of individuals (N < 500) have ever inherited wealth or received gifts when they were 12–20 years old. In short, focusing exclusively on parent–child dyads likely does not adequately capture the influence of wealth on young adult well-being (Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017; Pfeffer and Killewald 2018).

Theoretically, the direction of grandparental wealth toward grandchildren aligns with perspectives that stress the interconnectedness of families and the embeddedness of grandchildren within a multifaceted system (for a recent review, see Allen et al. 2019). Family systems (Kerr et al. 1988), life course (Elder et al. 2003), and social exchange (Thibaut and Kelley 1959) theories suggest that grandparents may play an important role in determining their grandchildren’s life chances. These models conceptually cohere around the proposition that families dynamically and reciprocally influence one other. The well-being of any given family member (e.g., a grandchild) is thus the product of family processes and interactions that unfold across both proximal and distal kin. Importantly, though, the grandparent–grandchild dyad and the parent–child dyad represent distinct familial ties (Hagestad 2006; King and Elder 1995; Silverstein and Marenco 2001). Thus, grandparents can provide assets directly to their grandchildren without filtering that provision through parents (Sadruddin et al. 2019).

Hällsten and Pfeffer (2017) argued that grandparental wealth serves three functions vis-à-vis grandchild well-being: it promotes investment, provides insurance against risks and communicates norms and behaviors. These three functions roughly parallel the instrumental, psychological, and symbolic benefits of parental wealth described earlier. Grandparental wealth can be used to invest in children by providing resources for financing education, accessing credit markets, or obtaining housing (Pfeffer and Killewald 2018). In addition, grandparental wealth can offer insurance (Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017), providing economic and psychological resources to counteract the uncertainty of young adulthood. Finally, grandparents offer cultural and social capital (Møllegaard and Jæger 2015) and often reinforce and transmit family values and norms (Prioste et al. 2017), thus influencing a young adult’s educational and family formation choices. These channels suggest that higher levels of grandparental wealth, like parental wealth, may be positively correlated with qualitatively better outcomes for young adults.

Insofar as grandparental wealth is a source of investment or insurance for young adults, it may be more salient for grandchildren whose parents have low levels of wealth (Anderson et al. 2018). Grandparents may calibrate their resource provision to grandchildren based on what parents can provide (Anderson et al. 2018). At the extreme, grandparents may provide resources only in times of crisis, such as when a parent dies or suffers a health crisis or unemployment (Cherlin and Furstenberg Jr 1992). Even in the absence of a crisis, however, grandparent resources may serve a compensatory function when parental resources are low (Mare 2011). This compensatory function may be particularly salient during the transition to young adulthood, when individuals face the steep costs of financing higher education or establishing a financially independent household.

Despite the likely salience of grandparental wealth for grandchild well-being, relatively few studies have directly assessed this association. A small body of work has investigated the intergenerational transmission of economic resources from grandparent to grandchild, finding that grandparental wealth predicts grandchild wealth or income, irrespective of parental net worth (Adermon et al. 2018; Pfeffer and Killewald 2018; Toney and Robertson 2021). These studies also documented the importance of in vivo transfers, finding that bequests and gifts explain only a small amount of variance in the grandparent-to-grandchild transmission of net worth (Pfeffer and Killewald 2018).

The only study to focus on grandparental wealth per se is that of Hällsten and Pfeffer (2017), which examined how grandparental wealth predicts 9th grade grandchildren’s academic performance. Using Swedish registry data, they found positive correlations between grandparental wealth and grandchildren’s grade point averages—an association that was statistically robust to the presence of parental wealth. Their study complements research using non-U.S. data (Deindl and Tieben 2017; Lehti et al. 2019; Møllegaard and Jæger 2015), which demonstrated positive correlations between grandparent socioeconomic status and financial resources and grandchildren’s educational achievement (for a recent review, see Anderson et al. 2018). Beyond the Hällsten and Pfeffer (2017) study, we are unaware of research investigating how grandparental wealth predicts grandchild well-being in childhood or young adulthood.

Some studies using European data have cast doubt on the importance of grandparents’ socioeconomic status in determining grandchildren’s well-being, arguing instead that parents’ socioeconomic standing fully accounts for any status transmission (Bol and Kalmijn 2016; Engzell et al. 2020). Although not focusing on wealth per se, this body of work suggests that concerns about three-generational economic mobility are overstated and that examining the grandparent–grandchild tie is noninformative. However, this work used data from countries with stronger social safety nets than the United States. Grandparental wealth may be more likely to provide a safety net for U.S. young adults when social safety nets are weak, especially when parental wealth levels are low.

### Present Study and Hypotheses

Our study provides the first estimates of the association between parental wealth during adolescence and a set of indicators important for the transition to adulthood. Based on the theoretically predicted and empirically documented contribution of wealth to familial well-being and positive child development (Diemer et al. 2020; Miller et al. 2021), we anticipate that:

#### Hypothesis 1:

Parental wealth will be positively correlated with educational attainment and employment and negatively correlated with nonmarital fertility and idleness in young adulthood.

In the absence of theoretical and empirical evidence, we assume that the strength of the association between parental wealth and young adult outcomes can be similar or can be different across outcomes.

We also examine the role of grandparental wealth in the transition to young adulthood. Given theoretical consistency regarding the relationship between grandparental and parental wealth and early adulthood outcomes (Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017), we expect that

#### Hypothesis 2:

Grandparental and parental wealth will have similarly signed associations with young adult outcomes.

However, given that grandparental wealth is a resource stream independent from parental wealth (Pfeffer and Killewald 2018), we also hypothesize that

#### Hypothesis 3:

The associations between parental versus grandparental wealth and young adult outcomes will be statistically independent from each other.

Finally, based on evidence suggesting that grandparent resources play a compensatory role in grandchild outcomes (Anderson et al. 2018), we suggest that

#### Hypothesis 4:

Grandparental wealth may be a stronger predictor of young adult outcomes when parental wealth is low and may be less important when parental wealth is high.

## Data and Methods

### Data

Data come from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), a nationally representative, longitudinal sample of U.S. households. The PSID’s multigenerational and longitudinal design, large sample size, and detailed data on wealth and outcomes for recent cohorts of young adults make it ideally suited for this study. We use all waves of data from 1968 to 2019. The PSID’s wealth measures have been shown to be reliable, despite underreporting of the wealthiest 3% (Pfeffer et al. 2016).

Our sample consists of households with a resident child aged 12–16 observed during PSID waves collecting wealth data (1984, 1984, 1989, 1994, and biannually from 1999 onward). We focus on children aged 12–16 because family resources at these ages may be critical to early-life success (Conger et al. 1994) and because it facilitates comparisons with other research (e.g.,Zhan and Sherraden 2011).1 Robustness checks (available upon request) using ages 10–14 and 10–17 produced findings consistent with our main results. Following previous studies examining the relationship between wealth and college attendance (Pfeffer 2018), we measure outcomes at age 20. Age 20 marks a significant juncture in the transition to adulthood, as it represents the midpoint of this transformative period. At this age, only a few respondents have already established their own households, with the majority still in the process of doing so (Pfeffer 2018). Respondents not observed at age 20 are used if they were observed at age 21. Age 20 respondents were born between 1968 and 1999. Robustness checks using age 25 give us generally consistent results (see Online Appendix S1). As discussed in further detail below, sample sizes ranged from 11,621 to 16,647 for the parent analyses, and 3,579 to 5,019 for the grandparent analyses.

### Measures

Our primary outcomes are college attendance, steady employment, idleness, and nonmarital fertility. All outcomes are measured as dichotomous indicators and are assessed at the wave when the respondent turned 20. College attendance indicates whether a respondent completed more than 12 years of schooling by age 20. Steady or full-time employment indicates whether an individual reported at age 20 having worked at least 910 hours per year2. Most of the individuals who had steady employment were not in school. An individual is considered to be idle if they had not been full-time employed or attended college at age 20. Nonmarital fertility measures whether an individual (either male or female) reports being a parent and not married, and his/her age becoming a parent was no older than 20. Table 1 shows weighted descriptive statistics for our sample. By age 20, 39.3% of individuals had attended college, 7.9% had a nonmarital birth, 31.4% had steady employment, and 23.3% were idle.

Wealth is the sum of a household’s fungible assets in the previous year (including home equity) minus debts, converted to 2018 dollars. Net assets include the value of business equity, bank deposits, stocks, financial securities, vehicles, primary residence, other real estate properties, and other miscellaneous assets not classified elsewhere. Net debts include credit card charges, education debts, medical or legal bills, loans from relatives, housing debts, business debts, and other debts not classified elsewhere. Wealth is measured both continuously in percentiles and in quartiles; quartiles account for potential nonlinearity in the association between family wealth and outcomes. Household wealth, as defined here, captures a child’s parental wealth.

To measure grandparental wealth, we first use PSID’s intergenerational mapping data set to match children to their paternal and maternal grandparents. We map each grandchild to each individual grandparent, and then find each grandparent’s household wealth. We sum wealth observed across grandparents and then calculate the average, rather than using the sum of grandparents’ household wealth, to avoid the problem of double counting (Two grandparents residing in the same household will have the same level of household wealth – say $100,000. But if we summed wealth across grandparents, the level of wealth would be $200,000, which is an obvious misrepresentation of their wealth). As a robustness check, we have alternatively used only one grandparent’s wealth instead of taking the average, and the results are highly consistent (see Appendix Table A1).

To account for economies of scale, we adjust net worth by the square root of household size (Altonji and Doraszelski 2005; Brady et al. 2020). Following Killewald et al. (2017)), we measure household wealth as a household’s percentile rank in the net worth distribution of a given year. Using the percentile rank of wealth rather than a log of wealth means that all households, even those with negative wealth, can be included in the model. Percentile net worth is calculated relative to all households with children aged 12–16 in the analytic samples in that year, weighted by PSID individual weights. Percentile net worth is then averaged over the years when children were aged 12–16; because wealth was not collected every year, children will vary in how many years parental wealth was observed. Robustness checks using wealth excluding home equity and wealth including only home equity generated findings consistent with our main results (see Online Appendix S2). Results measuring wealth using the inverse hyperbolic sine instead of percentiles were also consistent with our main findings. Results of these robustness checks are available upon request.

Covariates include respondent’s birth year, gender, race (White, Black, or other), and ethnicity (Hispanic or non-Hispanic); the parents’ highest educational attainment (less than high school, high school, college, college degree or more) and marital status (i.e., married vs. not married); and the number of children in the household.3 We also control for household income, measured as the sum of earnings, rents, child support, and other types of income in the previous year. Income is expressed in 2018 dollars using the Consumer Price Index. As with parental wealth, we adjust household income for the square root of household size and calculate it to be the weighted percentile rank in the income distribution of a certain year relative to all households with children aged 12–16 in the analytic samples in that year. We further construct childhood measures of the parents’ highest educational attainment, parents’ marital status, the number of children in the household, and percentile household income by taking averages of these time-varying measures across ages 12–16 to account for their average exposure effects (Brady et al. 2020). Because of high rates of missing data (at least 14% depending on outcomes), we did not include parental or grandparental age in our primary analyses. In supplementary analyses, we incorporated controls for the quadratic form of the oldest parent’s age and conducted analyses involving grandparental wealth, specifically accounting for the age of the oldest grandparent. Encouragingly, these supplementary analyses produced outcomes that are consistent with our principal findings (refer to Appendix Tables A2–A3 and Appendix Figure A1).

Our sample sizes vary by outcome because different outcomes have different missing patterns. After we exclude a small number of observations with missing covariate information, the sample sizes for the parental wealth analysis range from 11,621 to 16,647. These sample sizes are larger than those of other PSID-based wealth studies that examined respondents at older ages and used fewer waves of data (e.g., Brady et al. 2020; Pfeffer 2018). The sample size for the grandparental wealth analysis ranges from 3,579 to 5,019. Comparing the parent and grandparent samples, we find that the grandparent sample has slightly higher parental wealth levels than the parent sample (p = .09). Appendix Table A4 shows that the associations between continuously measured parental wealth and outcomes are consistent in the parent and grandparent samples, suggesting little evidence of sample selection bias. However, the associations between parental wealth quartile and non-educational outcomes are less robust in the grandparent sample than in the parent sample, possibly because parents are positively selected by wealth in the grandparent sample.

### Analytical Strategy

To examine the impact of family wealth on outcomes in early adulthood net of covariates, we model each outcome as a function of family wealth and the covariates using linear regressions with birth cohort fixed effects: (1) y i = β 0 + β 1 P W i + β 2 X i + ϵ i , where y i is the outcome at age 20, β 1 is the parameter of interest, and P W i captures parental wealth. Considering the significant cohort variations between wealth and educational outcomes documented in previous studies (Pfeffer 2018), we include birth cohort fixed effects to account for cohort-specific patterns between wealth and our outcomes. We first estimate a model with only the respondent’s birth year, gender, race and ethnicity as covariates because other covariates are possible mechanisms through which family wealth may affect outcomes during transition to adulthood (e.g., family wealth may affect the number of children in the household, which may affect college attendance). This model will give us an overall association between family wealth and outcomes. We then estimate another model controlling for all covariates. This model will give us the estimated association between family wealth and outcomes net of the possible mechanisms captured by the covariates. To account for selective attrition, we weight estimates using the longitudinal weight of the last observation in the sample for each individual. Robust standard errors are clustered at the original PSID household level. Results using logistic regression models generated consistent findings and are available upon request. We report results from the ordinary least squares regression models because the interpretation of those coefficients is more straightforward than the logistic regression coefficients.

In analyses using a subsample of respondents with available information on grandparental wealth, we estimate the following model: (2) y i = β 0 + β 1 P W i + β 2 G P W i + β 3 X i + ϵ i , where y i is the outcome at age 20, P W i captures parental wealth, and G P W i captures grandparental wealth. β 1 and β 2 are the parameters of interest.

To investigate the hypothesis that grandparental wealth is more important when parental wealth is low than when it is high, we modify the model in Eq. (2) by adding an interaction term between parental and grandparental wealth: (3) y i = β 0 + β 1 P W i + β 2 G P W i + β 3 P W i × G P W i + β 4 X i + ϵ i , where the term P W i × G P W i captures the interaction of the two wealth variables, and β 3 is our primary parameter of interst.

## Results

### Parental Wealth and Transition to Adulthood Outcomes

As shown in Table 2, parental wealth generally shows the anticipated beneficial association with young adult outcomes at age 20, except for steady employment. A one percentile increase in parental wealth is associated with small but positive changes in college attendance and small but negative changes in nonmarital birth, steady employment, and idleness (Panel A, Model 1). For example, a one percentile increase in parental wealth is associated with a 0.4 percentage point increase in the probability of college attendance (i.e., an additional 4 of every 1,000 respondents). These associations, with the exception of steady employment, are statistically robust to the inclusion of additional covariates capturing possible mechanisms through which parental wealth may affect outcomes (Model 2).4

Results for the parental wealth quartiles (Panel B) are consistent with the percentile results. Wealth is positively correlated with college attendance and negatively correlated with nonmarital births and idleness. Estimates also suggest a wealth gradient. We calculate the differences between consecutive quartiles’ coefficients to see if the same 25-percentile change5 in wealth ranking predicts the change in college outcomes, nonmartial birth and idleness differentially at different quartiles. We observe that moving from the third quartile to the fourth quartile is associated with the smallest change in all three outcomes. For college attendance and nonmarital birth, moving from second quartile to the third quartile is associated with the largest change in outcomes compared with any other consecutive quartile changes. Figure 1 helps visualize this wealth gradient. Coefficients are substantially attenuated once we include additional controls (Model 2) but suggest generally larger associations with outcomes at higher quartiles of parental income.

Results for employment are inconsistent across quartiles (a positive association for the second quartile and a negative association for the fourth quartile), but the inclusion of covariates yields estimates showing that wealth at the second and third quartiles is positively associated with employment.6 One possible explanation for the observed negative (and insignificant) coefficient for the fourth quartile is that children in wealthy families have less incentive to seek employment.

Results presented thus far indicate that parental wealth positively predicts college attendance and negatively predicts nonmarital births and idleness by age 20. Associations are nonlinearly increasing. Moving from the second quartile to the third quartile is associated with larger changes relative to moving from the bottom quartile to the second quartile or from the third quartile to the fourth quartile. Further, these associations are generally statistically robust to the inclusion of covariates, including parental education, family structure characteristics, and household income. Larger associations are observed for college attendance than for the other outcomes. The relationship between parental wealth and steady employment appears inconsistent before we control for covariates: less wealthy individuals are more likely to be employed full-time than more wealthy individuals. Net of income, parental education, and family structure characteristics, however, parental wealth positively predicts steady employment by age 20 for those with parental wealth at the second and third quartiles.

Our measures of employment and idleness largely preclude education; that is, fulltime employed adults are unlikely to be students enrolled in college, and they are not considered to be idle. Therefore, the observed associations between parental wealth and these outcomes cannot be driven by changes in college attendance. Additional analyses controlling for college attendance at age 20 when examining fertility outcomes at age 25 (available upon request) further confirm that the predictive power of parental wealth for nonmarital fertility is not merely a reflection of its predictive power for educational outcomes. We interpret these results to suggest that parental wealth may be important beyond its ability to directly purchase, for example, a college education. Instead, wealth likely informs young adults’ broader life path by establishing norms and expectations for non-educational outcomes.

### The Predictive Value of Grandparental Wealth

Models including grandparental wealth (Table 3) indicate that the predictive power of grandparental wealth varies by outcome.7 For college attendance, grandparental wealth is positively associated, albeit with coefficients that are substantively smaller than those for parental wealth. Additionally, including grandparental wealth has little influence on the association between parental wealth and college attendance. The coefficients associated with parental wealth (whether measured as percentiles or in quartiles) are in the same direction and of similar magnitude as the respective coefficients when grandparental wealth is not included (see Table 2). For example, when we control for grandparental wealth, a one percentile increase in parental wealth is associated with a 0.17 percentage point increase in college attendance (p < .01). When we do not adjust for grandparental wealth, the respective estimate is 0.18 percentage point (p < .01; Table 2, Model 2).

For non-educational outcomes except for nonmarital birth, grandparental wealth measured as percentiles or in quartiles is significantly predictive (grandparental wealth was not a significant predictor of nonmarital birth). A one percentile increase in grandparent’s wealth is associated with a 0.10 percentage point increase in steady employment and a 0.08 percentage point decrease in idleness at age 20 (p < .05 for both). Moreover, when grandparental wealth is included in the models of employment and idleness, the coefficients associated with parental wealth generally diminish and no longer reach conventional levels of statistical significance. For example, in models predicting idleness by age 20 (Table 2; Model 2), parental wealth measured in quartiles is associated with a decrease of 6.7 percentage points to 3.4 percentage points (depending on the quartile) relative to the first quartile in the likelihood of idleness (p < .05). When grandparental wealth is included, the respective coefficients decrease substantially in magnitude and no longer approach statistical significance, with the exception of the third quartile parental wealth. These results suggest that grandparental wealth may be more salient for those outcomes where the direct transfer of resources is less relevant (that is, purchasing a college education). Grandparental wealth may also predict outcomes that are informed by class status or expectations about the future, such as avoiding idleness.

Data limitations preclude a thorough investigation as to how grandparent wealth predicts outcomes, as we cannot explore the relative influence of grandparent co-residence or proximity (this data was only available after 2005). However, we were able to explore whether the outcomes were influenced by the presence of a living grandparent or positive grandparental wealth, rather than the specific amount of wealth involved (see Appendix Tables A5 and A6). Model results indicated that positive grandparental wealth predicts college attendance and idleness, while not predicting the other outcomes. Meanwhile, having a living grandparent is linked to steady employment and idleness, with no significant impact on the remaining two outcomes. These findings suggest that the presence of a living grandparent and possessing positive grandparental wealth may explain some of the variance observed in our primary results.

### How Grandparental Wealth’s Predictive Value Varies by Parental Wealth

Finally, we consider the interaction relationship between grandparental wealth and parental wealth. The results are graphed in Figure 2; model estimation results are shown in Appendix Table A7.

At age 20, associations between grandparental wealth and the outcomes are generally the greatest when parental wealth is lowest (Figure 1). For example, the predicted probability of attending college for young adults with parental wealth in the 1st percentile is approximately 0.24 when grandparental wealth is also in the 1st percentile. When grandparental wealth is in the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles, the predicted probability of attending college increases to 0.28, 0.33, and 0.37, respectively. When grandparental wealth is in the 99th percentile, the predicted probability of attending college is as high as 0.41. Consequently, for children with parental wealth in the lowest percentile, an increase in grandparental wealth from the 25th to the 75th percentile is associated with a 9 percentage points increase in the probability of attending college, from 0.28 to 0.37. However, as parental wealth increases, the predictive power of grandparental wealth decreases. These results suggest that grandparental wealth matters less for those with wealthier parents. In fact, for those with parental wealth above the 75th percentile, grandparental wealth hardly matters for college attendance (see Figure 2, displaying a tight clustering of colored lines on the right side of the college attendance graph). We find similar patterns for nonmarital births assessed at age 20, although the interaction term is not statistically significant. For employment and idleness, we also find that the predictive power of grandparental wealth on outcomes is strongest for those with lower parental wealth. Put differently, the predicted probabilities across quintiles of grandparental wealth diverge more among those with lower wealth parents. Findings are thus consistent with our hypothesis that grandparental wealth complements parental wealth, especially when the latter is limited.

Although the direction of the relationship between parental wealth and college attendance or nonmarital birth is consistent across grandparental wealth levels (i.e., slopes are positive for college attendance and negative for nonmarital birth), the direction of the relationship between parental wealth and steady employment or idleness differs across grandparental wealth levels. For example, higher parental wealth always predicts higher average college attendance, irrespective of grandparental wealth. The same result does not hold for steady employment or idleness: parental wealth predicts lower employment for those with high grandparental wealth (i.e., in the 99th percentile) but higher employment for those with low grandparental wealth. Similarly, parents’ wealth predicts higher idleness for those with high grandparental wealth but lower idleness for those with low grandparental wealth. Consequently, our results suggest that in some cases, grandparental wealth may entirely reverse the relationship between parental wealth and markers of the transition to adulthood.

## Conclusions and Discussion

Parental and grandparental wealth represent an important but overlooked component of kin support during emerging adulthood. Our study revealed four important findings. First, parental wealth is positively associated with college attendance, in line with previous studies (Conley 2001; Hardy and Marcotte 2020; Jez 2014). Consistent with Pfeffer (2018))’s findings, the associations we find are nonlinear. When controlling for a variety of household characteristics that could potentially mediate the relationship between parental wealth and educational outcomes, these patterns largely persisted despite smaller in magnitudes. The substantively large magnitude of this finding speaks to the relative predictive value of parents’ wealth for human capital attainment and supports arguments that parental wealth is an important driver of inequality (Killewald et al. 2017).

Second, we extend knowledge on the role of parental wealth in young adulthood by finding evidence that parental wealth shapes the transition to adulthood through both educational and non-educational makers of young adult success. Consistent with H1, we find that parental wealth is associated with increases in steady employment and decreases in idleness and early nonmarital fertility at age 20. As with the educational outcomes, associations are nonlinear. Magnitudes of the coefficients are modest but substantively similar across outcomes. When controlling for a variety of household characteristics that could potentially mediate the relationship between parental wealth and fertility and employment outcomes, these patterns largely persisted despite smaller in magnitudes. In this model (Model 2), high quartiles of wealth, relative to the first,

is associated with a 3 to 7 percentage points decrease in idleness, a 0.3 to 3 percentage points decrease in nonmarital birth (only for the third and fourth quartiles), and a 3 to 4 percentage points increase in steady employment (only for the second and third quartiles). Given that measures of employment and idleness largely exclude those in college, we argue that these findings underscore how parental wealth can predict outcomes where a direct transfer of resources is less relevant. Instead, wealth likely informs young adults’ broader life path by establishing norms and expectations; these norms and expectations speak not only to human capital attainment, but also to choices regarding employment and fertility.

Third, our study is one of the first to look beyond the role of parental wealth and investigate the independent roles of parental and grandparental wealth in predicting outcomes. Our H2 was that grandparent and parental wealth would have similar associations with outcomes, a hypothesis that was largely confirmed by results. We find that relative to parental wealth, grandparental wealth is more predictive of steady employment and idleness and is at least as predictive of nonmarital births. Findings support H3 and the argument that the grandparent–grandchild dyad represents a distinct tie from the parent–child dyad (Hagestad 2006; King and Elder 1995), with independent but similarly signed associations with the transition to adulthood. Although we could not investigate specific mechanisms in this study, we hypothesize that grandparental wealth may affect children through financial and economic pathways and through the transmission of cultural and social norms regarding desirable behavior. For example, grandparental wealth is more predictive of steady employment and idleness, perhaps because grandparental wealth may be more strongly associated with the likelihood of working for a family business or owning a business than parental wealth (Bacolod and Ranjan 2008; Pfeffer and Killewald 2018). Alternatively, grandparental wealth may better capture the transmission of norms in a family: grandparental wealth reinforces expected outcomes of young adults, such as working and avoiding a nonmarital birth.

Nonetheless, our findings reveal that grandparental wealth appears to matter less than parental wealth for educational outcomes. Results are consistent with previous studies suggesting that grandparents’ economic capital, net of parents’ economic capital, has little importance to grandchildren’s educational outcomes (Deindl and Tieben 2017; Lehti et al. 2019; Møllegaard and Jæger 2015). A range of mechanisms may explain these findings. Given the increasing importance of financial aid in U.S. tertiary education (Dynarski and Scott-Clayton 2013), families may seek to rely less on grandparental wealth to maximize aid receipts. Alternatively, given the likely greater involvement of parents in children’s educational activities (Zhan 2006), parents’ education-related expectations may be transmitted more effectively than those of grandparents. Although we cannot test these pathways, future research should aim to disentangle the reasons why grandparental wealth appears to matter for only some outcomes.

Finally, our study is the first to examine how parental and grandparental wealth interact in shaping young adults’ transition to adulthood. Consistent with H4, the associations between grandparent wealth and outcomes are generally the largest when parental wealth is low. Grandparental wealth matters when parental wealth is lacking (Anderson et al. 2018), acting as a buffer to the disadvantages associated with scarce parental resources. However, we also observe important complexities in the relationship between grandparental wealth and outcomes. In particular, having relatively wealthy grandparents reverses the association between parental wealth and employment-related outcomes (i.e., steady employment and idleness). Thus, higher parental wealth predicts worse employment outcomes among young adults with wealthy grandparents but better employment outcomes among those with poorer grandparents. Future research should build on our research by considering not only the independent role of grandparental wealth but also the nuanced ways in which it interacts with immediate (i.e., parental) resources.

Our paper is not without limitations. First, our results should not be interpreted as establishing a causal relationship. An observational dataset such as the PSID cannot assess all potential confounders between parental or grandparental wealth and young adults’ outcomes. In particular, the goal of our grandparental analyses is to describe the association between grandparental wealth and young adults’ outcomes net of parents’ wealth and other characteristics. To estimate the causal effect of grandparental wealth, one needs to account for potential collider bias (Breen 2018), measurement error in socioeconomic status across generations (Ferrie et al. 2021), and families’ demographic behavior such as births and deaths (Song 2021), which is beyond the scope of our study. In addition, to increase our sample size and obtain more powerful estimates, we forgo examining patterns across cohorts and instead implicitly estimate averages. Relatedly, because of data quality limitations, parents are positively selected in terms of wealth in our grandparents’ sample. Given our finding that grandparental wealth matters more when parental wealth is low, our analyses may underestimate the predictive power of grandparental wealth. Additionally, analyses of grandparental wealth may be biased for several reasons, including the nonrandomness of the number of grandparents observed for any given child (Engzell et al. 2020). Nevertheless, absent European-style registry data that can overcome some of these biases, the PSID is one of the few U.S. data sets that can be used to study the associations between grandparental wealth and child wellbeing.

Second, we also do not consider potentially important contextual factors that may interact with or mediate the effects of parental and grandparental wealth on outcomes. For example, neighborhood-level economic and social context and school characteristics are known to significantly influence young adults (Killewald et al. 2017; Yellen 2016). These factors may have complex relationships with parental and grandparental wealth and the outcomes we measure. Additionally, as the wealthiest families are underrepresented in PSID, our results do not capture the patterns for these families (Pfeffer et al. 2016).

Finally, a discussion of the influence of demographic heterogeneity on the observed associations is beyond the scope of this paper. However, in light of the racialization of American wealth (Darity and Mullen 2020), we examined how parental and grandparental wealth predict young adult well-being for non-Hispanic White and Black young adults separately in Online Appendix S3 (Small sample sizes precluded examining other racial/ethnic groups). For nonmarital birth and idleness, we found that grandparental wealth tends to be more important for Black than for White young adults. This finding is consistent with the idea that grandparental wealth serves a compensatory function, although further research is needed.

Our descriptive findings bear relevant implications for policymakers at a time of increasing attention on the role of early adulthood as a determinant of adult economic, social, and health success. Our results reinforce the notion that policies aimed at improving or equalizing young adults’ outcomes should target not only those outcomes directly (e.g., through in-school or labor market programs) but also the broader contextual mechanisms that drive divergences. In this context, growing debate centers on the desirability of policies aiming to address the financial and human capital endowments with which young people enter adulthood, such as a universal capital endowment (Derviş and Strauss 2020) or so-called baby bonds (Lowrey 2020). Our study should not be interpreted as reflecting on the effectiveness of these policies. However, it suggests the need for innovation to address the ingrained, cumulative drivers of unequal outcomes.

Moreover, our findings highlight the importance of shifting the focus beyond parental resources when developing policies targeting young adults’ outcomes. In particular, children and young adults’ parents and grandparents who are both low wealth grandparents might face amplified vulnerability. Thus, policies that improve the financial standing of older generations may also benefit young adults. Results of our supplementary analyses further suggest that such policies may especially benefit children of color. Given the prevalence of intergenerational disadvantages in the United States, it behooves us to remember that the successful transition to young adulthood is likely informed by the kin support of multiple generations.
